name: Phone at eye level / tech neck avoidance

lead: This habit means lifting your phone toward eye level so your head does not tilt down. People use it to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, and link it to a better neck line and jawline.

The chain is the phone held at eye level, less head-down neck flexion, then better neck posture. The reasoning is biomechanical: a head held forward and down loads the neck more than an upright head. A 2023 scoping review found that text neck lacks a consensus definition across the literature, and no study tests the habit or its appearance effect.

paras: People hold the phone higher, rest the elbows on the body or a desk, use a stand or phone holder, and take breaks from long head-down sessions. It is a behavior change that applies immediately to how the head is carried.
No notable risks are described. Holding a phone higher is a behavioral change only; arm fatigue is a practical downside.

angle.text: Holding the phone at eye level keeps the head up instead of down, which posture and looksmaxxing circles link to a better neck line and jawline. The path runs from the phone held high to less head-down flexion to better neck posture. Tech neck lacks an agreed definition, and the appearance link comes from anecdote.

lead: Holding a phone at eye level to avoid tech neck, also called text neck, is a posture habit meant to prevent the head-down, forward-head position associated with prolonged device use. In looksmaxxing and posture communities it is linked to neck posture and jawline appearance.
A 2023 scoping review found that text neck is widely called a global epidemic but lacks a consensus definition across the peer-reviewed literature [1].
Related work has examined questionnaires on symptoms and preventive measures [2], skin changes sometimes labeled tech neck lines [3], and posture changes in skeletal remains [4].
infobox: Text neck, tech neck, forward head posture

paras: A scoping review of peer-reviewed articles using the terms text neck or tech neck found inconsistent definitions, which the authors said challenges researchers and clinicians [1]. Wikipedia's article on forward head posture describes smartphone and laptop use as a commonly proposed contributor, presented as plausible rather than established causation [5].

No studies found testing holding a phone at eye level as an intervention. Related research exists. A 2025 pilot questionnaire study explored symptoms, posture and preventive measures such as breaks and ergonomic tools [2]. A 2023 open-label study examined a topical and device treatment for tech neck lines and wrinkles in Chinese women, addressing skin rather than posture [3]. A 2024 study examined instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization in tech neck [6]. A 2024 preprint compared bone changes at the skull base in modern and ancient populations in relation to tech neck posture [4]. Reviews in 2026 discussed tech neck as a spinal and orthodontic topic [7].

Wikipedia notes claims that head-forward posture increases neck load several-fold and ties it to neck pain, and cites a 2019 meta-analysis finding correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents; it does not discuss jawline or facial appearance [5].
